record.original_question: (Well-known problem). Does there exist a finitely presented(infinite) simple group requiring more than two generators? Cf. 6.44 in Archive.

evidence.quote: (Well-known problem). Does there exist a finitely presented(infinite) simple group requiring more than two generators? Cf. 6.44 in Archive.

artifact.self_contained_problem: Does there exist a finitely presented infinite simple group $G$ such that $G$ cannot be generated by two elements (equivalently, the minimal number of generators of $G$ is at least $3$)?
artifact.status_search_result: The question is listed as a well-known open problem in the Kourovka Notebook (cf. Archive 6.44). Web search did not surface a known finitely presented infinite simple group that provably requires more than two generators; all classical examples (Thompson's T, V, Burger–Mozes lattices, etc.) are 2-generated or not known to require 3 generators. The problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Unsolved problems in group theory. The Kourovka notebook.
status_evidence.snippet: Collection of unsolved problems in group theory, including questions about finitely presented simple groups.
status_evidence.claim: The Kourovka Notebook lists this as an open problem in group theory.

status_evidence.title: A Tour Around Finitely Presented Infinite Simple Groups
status_evidence.snippet: Survey of finitely presented infinite simple groups; known examples include Thompson's groups T, V and Burger–Mozes groups, all 2-generated.
status_evidence.claim: All commonly known finitely presented infinite simple groups are 2-generated, supporting that the problem remains unresolved.
